questions.q: What is a barren plateau, precisely?
options: A classical ML phenomenon unrelated to quantum circuits
A region of the parameter landscape where the gradient of the cost function vanishes exponentially (with qubit count) almost everywhere, stalling gradient-based training
A region where the gradient is always exactly zero by mathematical definition, regardless of circuit size
A hardware defect that only occurs on superconducting qubit chips
questions.explain: A barren plateau is a proven phenomenon where gradient variance shrinks exponentially as qubit count grows, making the landscape appear almost perfectly flat and swamping any true signal with sampling noise.

questions.q: What did McClean et al. (2018) actually prove, and why does this lesson treat it as unusually solid evidence compared to QML advantage claims?
options: That barren plateaus only affect circuits running on real hardware, never simulators

That gradient variance shrinks exponentially with qubit count for a broad class of expressive, randomly-initialized circuits -- a peer-reviewed, mathematically rigorous, widely confirmed result, unlike the much shakier practical-advantage claims
That QML always outperforms classical ML once circuits exceed 50 qubits
That quantum computers can never train any machine learning model
questions.explain: The 2018 Nature Communications result is a mathematically rigorous proof about gradient variance scaling, confirmed and extended by many follow-up papers -- one of the best-established facts in the field, in sharp contrast to unproven practical-advantage claims.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed in the lesson as a documented factor that worsens barren plateaus?
options: Random parameter initialization, and global cost functions measured across all qubits
Deeper, more expressive ansatze that approach the full Haar-random state space
Using fewer qubits than the circuit's number of trainable parameters
More qubits (the exponential shrinkage is specifically in qubit count)
questions.explain: The lesson lists more qubits, deeper/more expressive ansatze, random initialization, global cost functions, and hardware noise as documented worsening factors -- qubit-vs-parameter-count ratio alone is not one of them.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say none of the proposed mitigations (smarter initialization, local cost functions, shallower ansatze, problem-inspired ansatze) are a general solution to barren plateaus?
options: None of the mitigations have ever been tested on any circuit
Each helps in some regimes but trades away something else (model capacity, generality, or requires extra domain knowledge), and barren plateaus remain an open research problem
Barren plateaus were later proven not to be a real phenomenon, making mitigations unnecessary
Local cost functions completely eliminate barren plateaus in all cases with no tradeoffs
questions.explain: Each mitigation comes with a real, documented tradeoff -- shallower ansatze lose capacity, local cost functions constrain expressiveness, problem-inspired ansatze need domain knowledge -- which is why barren plateaus remain an open, unsolved research problem.

questions.q: A colleague wants to scale a randomly-initialized, generic hardware-efficient ansatz from 6 to 60 qubits expecting proportionally better accuracy. What should this lesson make you ask?
options: Nothing -- more qubits always straightforwardly improves training with no additional considerations
Whether they have enough classical RAM to store the state vector, which is the only relevant concern
Whether the circuit uses Qiskit or PennyLane, since that alone determines whether barren plateaus occur
How they plan to avoid or survive the exponential gradient-vanishing effect of barren plateaus at that qubit count, given it's a proven obstacle for exactly this kind of circuit
questions.explain: Scaling a randomly-initialized, generic, expressive ansatz to many more qubits is exactly the regime where McClean et al.'s proven barren plateau result applies most severely -- the colleague's claim needs to directly address this documented obstacle.
